name: Carlos Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Carlos, 43, with a bachelor’s degree in music. I’ve played clarinet in the town concert band for years, record practice parts for the music school and teach intermediate pupils on Mondays and Thursdays. I’m a dependable player rather than the strongest soloist. I like hearing the whole wind section settle on one pitch; I get tired of correcting late invoices after a concert.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household count on from that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at the library on regular hours, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is ordinary for a musician, with about four months of expenses saved. There are some other band and teaching posts nearby, but they are not vacancies until somebody advertises them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band that a tidier booking office is fine if the rehearsal and concert fees still arrive. Players still have to hear each other rather than obey a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library wage and our four-month reserve make an ordinary delayed concert manageable. I still watch the mortgage and the children’s activity fees, but neither is hanging on one recording date this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the Monday and Thursday lessons, the concert band chair and monthly practice-part recordings. This week I’d ask the school for next term’s paid lesson hours in writing, and through the first year I’d put one cleared recording fee each month into the mortgage reserve when bookings allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household in this mild picture. A late invoice is irritating, not a reason to cancel a child’s club today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What ordinary cost keeps you alert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school trip is the next large bill, and I know its due date. Four months saved gives us room to plan for it, though I would rather earn the money than use the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not use software for your lesson notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool. My written lesson book tells me what each child struggled with last week, and I can explain it without putting their playing online.

say: I would accept a tidier **booking office** while keeping rehearsal and concert fees visible.
I would tell players that **listening together** still matters in the band.
think: A steady **library wage** and four-month reserve make a late invoice manageable.
The **mortgage and school trip** still have known payment dates.
do: Keep **school lessons**, band chair and practice-part recordings through first year.
Get written **paid hours** now and save one cleared recording fee monthly when bookings allow.
feel: I feel **calm** about ordinary bills in this mild picture.
S0.quote: A late invoice is irritating, not a reason to cancel a child’s club today.
fieldNote: His **typical pay** and four-month cushion make one delayed concert tolerable while the library wage remains steady.
He **never uses AI**, keeping pupil notes in a written lesson book.

steps.text: Keep Monday and Thursday lessons, band chair and monthly practice-part recordings
Save one cleared recording fee monthly if bookings allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band that cheap practice tracks could make our school recording fees smaller. I’d ask the musicians’ union to set a minimum recording fee and clear permission before schools reuse our playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice parts bring about a quarter of my music pay. Losing those would not end my band chair, but it would slow our mortgage payments and the children’s activities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the school which practice parts it still pays for and take the issue to the union’s next meeting. In the first year, if orders fall, I’d add an intermediate pupil on Thursday only if the school has a paid place and my partner can cover pickup, and stop paying for the outside rehearsal room on unused days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about a real cut to my income. The reserve buys a few months of choice. A quarter of my music pay cannot disappear every year without a change at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fee would shrink first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first lost fee would be a clarinet guide for a student ensemble. It is enough for one of our children’s club bills, so I would track the orders each term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union ask for exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for a minimum per recorded part and consent for any reuse beyond the original class. The music school should be able to say what it pays for and what it keeps.

I would warn that cheap **practice tracks** may lower school recording pay.
think: Recorded parts provide about **one-quarter** of my music income.

do: Ask the **school** about paid orders and raise recording terms with the union this month.
Add a paid **Thursday pupil** only if school space and partner pickup are confirmed.
Stop paying for the **outside room** in first year if orders fall and days go unused.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a quarter of income could shrink despite savings.
S1.quote: A quarter of my music pay cannot disappear every year without a change at home.
fieldNote: The threatened **practice guides** are a real quarter of income, separate from the live chair.
Additional **school hours** stay tagged as current work and require paid space plus pickup.

steps.text: Ask union for minimum guide fees and recording consent this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AGI by 2028 could write practice parts and lesson plans cheaply, while robots that play hands-on work follow around 2031. I would not mistake those extra years for a guarantee of concert fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recorded guides could end in 2028, and some pupils may try a tool instead of lessons. My partner’s library wage and four months saved help, but they cannot replace my entire music income for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d ask the school for written paid hours and the band for booked concert fees. In the first year after AGI arrives, if practice orders stop, I’d cancel the unused rehearsal room at renewal, ask the union about recording rights, and audition for an advertised local band chair only if its written net fee covers travel and childcare; I’d keep current lessons until a written offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about those weekday fees, though I could still act. There are a few nearby bands, but an audition is not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes before robots can play clarinet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paper and recording work faces 2028 first. My breath and fingers might still earn concert fees until capable robots arrive around 2031, but the band books only so many evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a lower-paid post to keep working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take a post that leaves us worse off after travel and a sitter. If a band offers only a good title, I would keep my current chair and ask for the actual net amount.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from robot players around 2031.
I would keep asking for **written concert fees**, not assume live work survives.
think: Recorded guides and some **pupil lessons** could end by 2028.
A **four-month reserve** cannot replace my full music pay indefinitely.
do: Keep **school lessons** until a written band offer; confirm paid hours and concert fees before 2028; ask union if guides stop.
Cancel **unused room rent** at renewal in first year after 2028 if guides stop.
Seek **posted band chair** first post-2028 year if guides stop and written net fee covers travel and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about weekday pay, with a few months to act.
S2.quote: There are a few nearby bands, but an audition is not a job.
fieldNote: He expects **2028 thinking tasks** to change before capable robot players arrive around 2031.
His **band move** requires a genuine advertised opening and net pay after travel and childcare.

steps.text: Keep school lessons until written band offer; confirm paid hours and concert fees before 2028
Cancel unused rehearsal room at renewal first year after 2028 if guides stop
Ask union about recorded-part rights if practice orders stop after 2028
Audition for posted chair if guides stop after 2028; written net fee covers travel/childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the union that five years gives us time to get recorded-part rights in writing and try more live teaching. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031, with capable robot clarinetists around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could make adult ensemble coaching a useful second income, but it needs people willing to pay. I am not going to move four months of savings into a room deposit to test a theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask the independent community library for a free evening room and offer an eight-week clarinet circle only if eight adults prepay enough for my time and my partner can manage pickup. In the first year after 2031, I’d continue the circle only if eight still pay and the room remains free; I’d keep the school lessons while families book them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the longer-term recording fees, but I can test a class before signing anything big. Our current work and savings give us that space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test over five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight prepaid places would cover my time and basic printed music. If only five register or the library asks for a deposit, I would cancel before the mortgage reserve pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you renting a room for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not rent a room because a deposit would come from our mortgage reserve before a single adult pays. If the library cannot offer space without a deposit, I would postpone the circle and keep the paid school lessons. I would pay a local helper only if registrations cover that fee too.

say: I would seek written **recording rights** through the union before 2031.
I would remind players that capable **robots** follow thinking AGI around 2034.
think: Adult **coaching** could replace recording pay only if enough people pay.
I would not spend the **mortgage reserve** on a hall deposit.
do: Ask the library for a **free room** next spring; require eight prepayments for teaching and a partner pickup plan.
Pay any **local helper** only if registrations cover their fee; repeat after 2031 only with eight payments and a free room.
Keep **school lessons** while families continue booking.
feel: I feel **anxious** about future guides, with time to test paid coaching.
S3.quote: I am not going to move four months of savings into a room deposit to test a theory.
fieldNote: The separate **library circle** relies on a free room, eight prepaid adults and partner pickup.
He uses the **union** to negotiate reuse terms rather than relying on one player’s bargaining power.

steps.text: Start eight-week circle with free library room, eight prepayments covering teaching, and partner available for pickup
Pay local helper only if registrations cover their fee
Repeat circle first post-2031 year only if eight pay and room stays free
Keep school lessons while paid families continue booking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that a decade is time to learn work they enjoy and ask whether it pays. Thinking AGI in 2036 and robot players around 2039 are different dates, but written fees matter now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI reaches the written parts and about 56 when capable robots arrive. The mortgage may still be there, though my partner’s steady wage and our reserve make the next few years manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the band chair and school lessons and save a share of each paid guide fee when it clears. Over the decade I’d run the adult circle only with a free room, eight prepayments covering my time and pickup covered; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep paid classes and concerts while booked and seek an advertised music-school post if guides stop, the school accepts my degree and experience, and the written net wage covers travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about music in the far future, not frightened about this month. Four months saved is useful if we keep adding to it, but it is not a retirement fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the decade change for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would transfer one fifth of each cleared guide fee after travel into a separate mortgage account. If those fees stop, I would not pretend the transfer still happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing at 56?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep playing while the band pays and my hands hold up. A robot clarinetist at 56 would not make me retired by law or by choice.

I would keep **2036 thinking AGI** distinct from robot clarinetists around 2039.

Run **adult circle** only with free room, eight prepayments covering teaching and confirmed pickup.

feel: I feel **uneasy** about far-future music work, not this month’s bills.
S4.quote: Four months saved is useful if we keep adding to it, but it is not a retirement fund.
fieldNote: His **moderate reserve** supports a careful class test without funding a hall deposit.
He ties **saving** to cleared guide fees and any new school move to written net pay.

Save fifth of each cleared guide fee after travel while guides sell

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recorded guides could end before paid classes grow enough. A written school-hours promise, an advertised band chair with net pay that covers pickup, and enforceable recording rights would help. I have savings for a gap, not for years without music income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how the players know whether a guide was useful. A pupil who comes back and plays one clean phrase is better evidence than a file download count.

headlineQuote: A pupil who comes back and plays one clean phrase is better evidence than a file download count.
portrait: Carlos is a **43-year-old clarinetist** with a music bachelor’s, years in a town band, school teaching and recorded practice parts.
Typical **music pay**, a steady library wage and four months saved support two children and a mortgage.
He **never uses AI** and uses written fees, union consent and existing lessons before any career change.
Fast AGI threatens **recorded guides** before robot players arrive, while a separate prepaid library circle may replace fees.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could end guide income before paid teaching expands.
whatWouldHelp: Written **school hours**, a real band vacancy at net pay covering pickup and enforceable recording rights would help.
